questions.title: Complement conditions
questions.markdown:
Which pair of conditions defines a complement $b$ of $a$ in a Boolean algebra?

**(A)** $a\lor b=0,\ a\land b=1$

**(B)** $a\lor b=1,\ a\land b=0$

**(C)** $a\lor b=a,\ a\land b=b$

**(D)** $a=b$
questions.solution: **Correct option: (B).** A complement joins with the element to give 1 and meets with it to give 0.

questions.title: Complement uniqueness
questions.markdown:
How many complements does each element of a Boolean algebra have?

**(A)** None

**(B)** At least two

**(C)** Infinitely many

**(D)** Exactly one
questions.solution: **Correct option: (D).** Complement existence is a Boolean-algebra property, and distributivity gives uniqueness.

questions.title: Boolean simplification
questions.markdown:
Which expression equals $a\lor(\neg a\land b)$?

**(A)** $a\lor b$

**(B)** $a\land b$

**(C)** $\neg a\lor b$

**(D)** $a$
questions.solution: **Correct option: (A).** Distribution gives $(a\lor\neg a)\land(a\lor b)=1\land(a\lor b)=a\lor b$.

questions.title: Disjunctive normal form
questions.markdown:
Which expression is in disjunctive normal form (a disjunction of conjunctions of literals)?

**(A)** $(x\lor y)\land z$

**(B)** $\neg(x\lor y)$

**(C)** $(x\land y)\lor(\neg x\land z)$

**(D)** $(x\lor y)\land(\neg x\lor z)$
questions.solution: **Correct option: (C).** $(x\land y)\lor(\neg x\land z)$ is an OR of two AND terms of literals.

questions.title: Conjunctive normal form
questions.markdown:
Which expression is in conjunctive normal form (a conjunction of disjunctions of literals)?

**(A)** $(x\land y)\lor z$

**(B)** $(x\lor y)\land(\neg x\lor z)$

**(C)** $\neg(x\land y)$

**(D)** $(x\land y)\lor(\neg x\land z)$
questions.solution: **Correct option: (B).** $(x\lor y)\land(\neg x\lor z)$ is an AND of two OR clauses of literals.

questions.title: Divisibility poset and antichains
questions.markdown: Draw the Hasse diagram for A = {1, 2, 3, 12, 18, 36}, ordered by divisibility: a is related to b iff a divides b. Is it a lattice? Justify. List all antichains of length more than one.
questions.solution:
The cover relations are $(1,2),(1,3),(2,12),(2,18),(3,12),(3,18),(12,36),(18,36)$. They determine the Hasse diagram below; line crossings without a labelled vertex are not additional elements.



![image](/midsem/figures/hasse-ensemble.png)



This poset is **not a lattice**. The common upper bounds of 2 and 3 are 12, 18 and 36. The two minimal common upper bounds 12 and 18 are incomparable, so there is no least upper bound. Equivalently, 12 and 18 have no greatest lower bound in the set: 2 and 3 are incomparable maximal common lower bounds. It is not valid to import gcd 6 into the set, since 6 is absent.

The complete list of antichains with more than one element is $\boxed{\{2,3\},\ \{12,18\}}$. Every other distinct pair is comparable, so there are no larger antichains.

questions.title: Bounded item selection
questions.markdown:
How many ways are there to select a total of 15 items from three types, subject to these limits?

Type A: 1 to 4 items; Type B: 3 to 7 items; Type C: 5 to 10 items.
questions.solution:
Let $u=A-1$, $v=B-3$, $w=C-5$. Then $u+v+w=6$, with $0\le u\le3$, $0\le v\le4$, $0\le w\le5$. The unrestricted nonnegative count is $\binom82=28$.

Subtract violations: $u\ge4$ contributes $\binom42=6$, $v\ge5$ contributes $\binom32=3$, and $w\ge6$ contributes $\binom22=1$. Intersections are impossible because their minimum sums exceed 6. Thus
``` math
\boxed{28-6-3-1=18}.
```
Items of the same type are indistinguishable, so this counts feasible triples of quantities, not arrangements.

questions.title: Partition bijection
questions.markdown: Show that the number of partitions of n with no part smaller than 3 equals the number of partitions of n+3 whose three largest parts are consecutive integers.
questions.solution:
For positive n, let $\lambda$ be a partition of n with every part at least 3. In its Ferrers diagram, the first three columns have the same height k. Its conjugate partition $\mu=\lambda'$ therefore satisfies $\mu_1=\mu_2=\mu_3=k$.

Define a new partition
``` math
\nu=(\mu_1+2,\mu_2+1,\mu_3,\mu_4,\ldots).
```
Its total is $n+3$, and its three largest parts are $k+2,k+1,k$, which are consecutive.

Conversely, if a partition of $n+3$ has largest parts $k+2,k+1,k$, subtract 2 from the first part and 1 from the second. The resulting partition has three equal largest parts k and total n. Conjugating it gives a partition of n in which every row has at least three cells, hence every part is at least 3. These constructions undo each other, proving the claimed equality. For n=1 or 2, both sets are empty.

questions.title: The 75th Fike permutation
questions.markdown: Find the 75th permutation of the five marks 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 in Fike’s order.
questions.solution:
Use the original descending-exchange Fike convention, with the original arrangement 01234 counted as permutation 1. Enumerate $(d_2,d_3,d_4,d_5)$ with $d_k=k,k-1,\ldots,1$, and $d_5$ varying fastest. For each tuple, start from 01234 and exchange positions k and $d_k$ in increasing k order, using one-based positions.

The zero-based index is $75-1=74$. The block weights for these four choices are 60, 20, 5 and 1:
``` math
74=1(60)+0(20)+2(5)+4(1).
```
Thus $(d_2,d_3,d_4,d_5)=(2-1,3-0,4-2,5-4)=\boxed{(1,3,2,1)}$.



| Exchange          | Arrangement |
|:------------------|:------------|
| Start             | 01234       |
| Positions 2 and 1 | 10234       |
| Positions 3 and 3 | 10234       |
| Positions 4 and 2 | 13204       |
| Positions 5 and 1 | 43201       |



Hence the answer under this convention is $\boxed{43201}$.

Convention reference: J. S. Rohl, “Programming Improvements to Fike’s Algorithm for Generating Permutations,” The Computer Journal 19(2), 156–159 (1976), Figure 1 and recursive procedure. <https://doi.org/10.1093/comjnl/19.2.156>. The convention is stated explicitly because Fike order is not lexicographic order.

questions.title: Regular self-complementary graph
questions.markdown: Show that if G is a regular self-complementary graph of order n, then n = 4t + 1 for some integer t.
questions.solution:
Assume a nonempty simple graph. If G is r-regular on n vertices, its complement is $(n-1-r)$-regular. Isomorphism to its complement implies
``` math
r=n-1-r,\qquad r=(n-1)/2.
```
Therefore n is odd. The handshake lemma says $nr=2|E|$ is even. Since n is odd, r must be even; write $r=2t$. Substitution gives $n=2r+1=\boxed{4t+1}$, with $t\ge0$.

questions.title: Minimum degree forces connectivity
questions.markdown: If G has p vertices and minimum degree $\delta$(G) $\ge$ (p - 1)/2, prove that G is connected.
questions.solution:
Suppose G is disconnected, and a component has s vertices. A vertex in that component has degree at most $s-1$, so
``` math
s-1\ge\delta(G)\ge(p-1)/2,\quad s\ge(p+1)/2.
```
Every component must satisfy this bound. Two components would already contain at least $p+1$ vertices, contradicting the total p. Hence G is connected. This argument assumes the usual simple-graph setting; a one-vertex graph is connected directly.
